title: Sita and the fire
hookLine: Sita walks into the flame and out
carry: agni, the witness: why vows are made at the fire

lines: THE REUNION THE STORY RAN TOWARD.
cards: This is the scene people stop at. The war is won. Sita is brought out of Lanka, after all those months in the garden refusing Ravana every day.
The whole army crowds around to see her. She comes to Rama. This is the reunion the entire story has been running toward.
And it goes wrong. This one doesn't get tidied up. Here it is straight, then what people in the tradition have said about it, because they've been arguing about this scene for a very long time.

teach.b: In Valmiki's telling, Rama speaks coldly, in front of everyone. He says he fought to wipe out the insult to his name, and that since she lived in another man's house, he can't simply take her back.
She's free to go wherever she likes. Sita is stunned.
Then she answers him, and her answer is magnificent: her heart was always his; what Ravana did to her body was done by force; how could he speak to her like a common man?

teach.h: SITA ANSWERS, AND WALKS INTO THE FIRE.
teach.b: She turns to Lakshmana and tells him to build a fire, and she walks into the flames. The fire god, Agni, rises out of them carrying her unharmed, and declares her pure.
Rama says he never doubted her; he did it, he says, so the world would have no doubt. That's the text: agni pariksha, the trial by fire. Now, how the tradition reads it.

teach.h: SHADOW SITA, FLAW, OR TEST? ALL INSIDE.
teach.b: Tulsidas, in the Ramcharitmanas, tells it differently: before the abduction, the real Sita was placed in the fire's keeping, and a shadow Sita was the one taken; the fire only gives the real one back.
Some devotees take comfort in that. Others read Valmiki's scene as a king bowing to public opinion, and hold that as a flaw, or a tragedy, or a test of dharma under pressure.
Women have long sung and retold this story from Sita's side, questioning Rama, like the Bengali poet Chandrabati. None of these voices is outside Hinduism. They're all inside it.
This tradition doesn't ask you to stop asking. And one thing every telling keeps: the fire as witness.
Agni sees what's true, and it is Agni who speaks for Sita. That's why, at a Hindu wedding, the couple walks around a sacred fire: the vows are made with Agni as witness.

how: Sita's trial by fire is told and debated openly in Hindu homes, temples and scholarship; devotional tellings such as Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas present a shadow Sita, while some readers, poets and women's song traditions have questioned the scene from Sita's side.

o: Sita's walk into the fire to answer Rama's doubt
a fire ritual Rama lit to thank the gods
the burning of Lanka by Hanuman's lit tail

games.q: what's inside the scene — tap the pairs.
p: fire as witness, at every wedding
the shadow Sita was the one taken
a Bengali poet who told it from Sita's side

s: Sita walks into the fire silently
in Valmiki she answers Rama first, with dignity, then asks Lakshmana to build the fire.
every Hindu tradition tells this scene the same way
Valmiki, Tulsidas and later tellers tell it differently, and readers still argue.
in Valmiki, Agni himself carries Sita out of the flames
the fire god rises from the flames with her unharmed and declares her pure.

games.q: at a cousin's wedding, a friend asks why the couple walks around a fire. what fits today's story?
o: Agni is the witness: the fire that spoke for Sita sees the vows too.
the fire is just there for warmth and light.
it's to test the bride, like Sita.
games.why: Hindu wedding vows are made with Agni as witness, the same fire god who carried Sita out and said she was true. the trial scene itself is still argued over.

practice: Don't decide what the scene means; picture Sita walking toward the fire with her back straight, and Rama watching, and let yourself feel whatever comes: anger, confusion, awe, sadness, all felt by people who love this story.
Hold the question gently, like something you'll carry, not solve.

wordCard.voice: Agni pariksha. The trial by fire. Sita walks into the flame and out, and the argument about it has never stopped.

orig.note: Sanskrit: agni (fire) + pariksha (test). In Hindi today, pariksha also means a school exam.

carryVoice: Your line: Agni, the witness: why vows are made at the fire. The question about Sita can stay open. Sixty-eight, and counting.
